questions.prompt: A project lead must create and manage all resources in a resource group but must not be able to grant anyone else access. Which built-in role should you assign?
options: Owner
Contributor
User Access Administrator
Role Based Access Control Administrator
questions.explanation: Contributor grants full management of all resources, and its NotActions remove Microsoft.Authorization write and delete, so it can't create role assignments.
why_not: Owner can also assign roles, which the requirement forbids.
User Access Administrator manages access, not resources: it has only read access to resources.
This role assigns roles and reads resources; it can't create or manage them.
questions.clue: "create and manage all resources" but "not grant access": Contributor, not Owner.

questions.prompt: A security team member must assign Azure roles to others in a subscription but must not manage Azure Policy or any resources. What is the least-privileged built-in role?
options: Owner
User Access Administrator
Contributor
Role Based Access Control Administrator
questions.explanation: Role Based Access Control Administrator can only create and delete role assignments (plus read). Microsoft documents that it can't manage access in other ways, such as Azure Policy.
why_not: Owner manages every resource and every authorization setting: far more than needed.
User Access Administrator holds all of Microsoft.Authorization, which includes managing access through Azure Policy.
Contributor manages resources and can't assign roles at all.
questions.clue: "assign Azure roles" but "not manage Azure Policy": the narrower Role Based Access Control Administrator.

questions.prompt: A user holds Contributor on a subscription. They try to assign an Azure Policy definition to a resource group and the operation fails. Why?
options: Contributor's NotActions exclude Microsoft.Authorization write and delete operations, which include policy assignments
Contributor can't read policy definitions
Policy assignments require a Microsoft Entra role
Policies can only be assigned at management group scope
questions.explanation: Contributor's NotActions remove Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write and */Delete. That covers role assignments and policy assignments and definitions.
why_not: Contributor can read everything; writing the assignment is what's excluded.
Policy assignments are Azure resources governed by Azure RBAC, not Entra roles.
Policies can be assigned at management group, subscription, resource group or resource scope.
questions.clue: "Contributor" trying to assign a policy: policy assignments are Microsoft.Authorization writes.

questions.prompt: A user holds Contributor on a resource group. Contributor's NotActions exclude Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write. The same user is also assigned User Access Administrator on the same resource group. Can the user create role assignments on that resource group?
options: No, Contributor's NotActions take precedence over other roles
No, a user can't hold two privileged roles at the same scope
Yes, because Azure RBAC is additive and NotActions is not a deny
Only after a deny assignment is removed
questions.explanation: Effective permissions are the union of all applicable role assignments. NotActions only trims a wildcard within one role; it isn't a deny rule. User Access Administrator grants Microsoft.Authorization/*, so the user can assign roles. Only a deny assignment would block it.
why_not: NotActions only trims one role's wildcard. It never removes a permission granted by another role.
Nothing prevents holding several roles at one scope; their permissions add up.
The scenario has no deny assignment. A deny assignment would block the action, not be required to allow it.
questions.clue: "also assigned User Access Administrator": RBAC adds permissions across assignments; NotActions isn't a deny.

questions.prompt: You must give a support group read access to every resource group in three subscriptions, including resource groups created in the future. The subscriptions share a management group. What should you do?
options: Assign Reader to the group on each existing resource group
Assign Reader to the group at the management group scope
Assign Reader to each user at each subscription scope
Assign the Directory Readers Microsoft Entra role
questions.explanation: Assignments inherit to every child scope, including ones created later. One group assignment at the management group covers all three subscriptions.
why_not: Assignments on existing resource groups don't reach resource groups created later, and it multiplies the assignments to maintain.
That works but multiplies assignments per user. Group assignments at a higher scope are simpler and count once.
Microsoft Entra roles don't grant access to Azure resources.
questions.clue: "three subscriptions", "including future resource groups", "share a management group": assign once, at the management group.

questions.prompt: A Global Administrator can't see any subscriptions in the Azure portal. They need to grant themselves access to fix a subscription. What should they do first?
options: Assign themselves Owner from the subscription's Access control (IAM) page
Nothing: Global Administrator already has Owner on every subscription
Assign themselves the Privileged Role Administrator Microsoft Entra role
Turn on Access management for Azure resources in Microsoft Entra ID properties
questions.explanation: Elevating access assigns that user User Access Administrator at root scope (/), which lets them assign roles in any subscription. They should turn it off after the fix.
why_not: Without any Azure role they can't open the subscription's Access control page to assign anything.
By default the Global Administrator has no access to Azure resources.
That is another directory role; it grants nothing on Azure resources.
questions.clue: "Global Administrator can't see any subscriptions": elevate access first; Entra roles don't reach Azure resources.

questions.prompt: An application's managed identity needs to read blob data in one storage account and nothing else. Which assignment follows least privilege?
options: Reader on the subscription
Storage Blob Data Reader on the storage account
Owner on the storage account
Contributor on the resource group
questions.explanation: Reading blob contents is a data action. It needs a data role, such as Storage Blob Data Reader, at the narrowest scope that works: the storage account.
why_not: Reader is control plane only and far too broad in scope; it doesn't grant blob data access.
Owner has no DataActions and is privileged; it's the wrong kind of role and too much of it.
Contributor manages resources but has no DataActions, and the scope is broader than needed.
questions.clue: "read blob data" and "one storage account": a data role, scoped to that account.

questions.prompt: You remove a user's Reader assignment on resource group RG1. An hour later the user can still view RG1. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Role assignment changes take up to 24 hours
The user has another assignment that applies to RG1, inherited from a parent scope or received through a group
Deleted role assignments are soft-deleted for 30 days
Reader access can't be removed from a resource group
questions.explanation: Access is the union of every applicable assignment: direct, through groups, and inherited from the subscription or management group. Check access at RG1 shows them.
why_not: Changes take up to 10 minutes, and an hour has passed.
Role assignments aren't soft-deleted; removing one revokes it.
Any role assignment can be removed.
questions.clue: "still can view RG1" after removal: another assignment reaches RG1, inherited or through a group.

questions.prompt: `az role assignment list --assignee avery@contoso.com` returns an empty list, yet Avery can restart virtual machines in RG1. Which addition is most likely to reveal the assignment?
options: --output table
--include-classic-administrators
--all --include-inherited --include-groups
--role Contributor
questions.explanation: By default the command shows only direct assignments at the current subscription. --all adds child scopes such as RG1, --include-inherited adds parent scopes, and --include-groups adds assignments received through group membership.
why_not: Changing the format doesn't change which assignments are returned.
Classic administrator roles are retired; that isn't where modern access comes from.
Filtering by role still only shows direct assignments at subscription scope.
questions.clue: "empty list" yet the user has access: the assignment is inherited or comes through a group.

questions.prompt: In the Azure portal you open Access control (IAM) > Check access on a subscription for a user who holds Contributor on one resource group inside it. What do you see for that user?
options: Nothing from that resource group assignment; Check access shows assignments at the selected scope and inherited to it, not those at child scopes
The Contributor assignment, marked as a child-scope assignment
Contributor on the whole subscription
An error, because Check access only works on resource groups
questions.explanation: Check access lists role and deny assignments at the chosen scope and inherited from above. To see a child-scope assignment, run Check access at that resource group, or list with --all.
why_not: Check access doesn't list assignments at child scopes.
Assignments inherit downwards, never upwards.
Check access works at management group, subscription, resource group and resource scopes.
questions.clue: "Check access on a subscription" for a resource-group assignment: Check access lists assignments at that scope and above.
